Welcome. I’m really glad you’re here with me for this thought-provoking journey.
Today, we’ll walk together through a landscape that’s as challenging as it is fascinating—the space where existence and nonexistence meet.
Imagine, for a moment, questioning something as fundamental as bringing new life into the world. That’s exactly what David Benatar does in his eye-opening work, Better Never to Have Been: The Harm of Coming into Existence.
Benatar’s perspective invites us to look closely at an idea that might feel unsettling, yet incredibly important: is birth itself actually a harm? It’s a bold challenge to the common belief that life is always good, urging us to reconsider what we take for granted about being alive.
Together, we’ll unpack this radical argument—one that’s built on the idea that the absence of suffering is always a good thing, but the absence of pleasure isn’t necessarily bad. It’s a subtle distinction, but it changes the whole conversation around procreation, responsibility, and what it really means to bring someone into existence.
As we explore, you’ll notice how this philosophy weaves through ethical dilemmas, philosophical puzzles, and the raw realities of human experience. We’ll pause to think about harm, consent, and even the meaning of life itself—questions that aren’t just abstract, but touch each of us in deeply personal ways.
So, as we open the pages of Benatar’s challenging book, let’s keep an open mind and a willingness to question what we’ve always believed. By the end, you might just find yourself looking at the world—and your place in it—a little differently.
